title: Time series generation for option pricing on quantum computers using tensor network
abstract_summary: The paper proposes using Matrix Product States (MPS), a tensor network generative model, to produce joint time-series distributions of asset prices for path-dependent option pricing on quantum computers. The authors train MPS on simulated Heston-model paths and show that the model can generate realistic price paths and be used to price several path-dependent options, highlighting MPS as a promising approach to efficient quantum state preparation for quantum Monte Carlo option pricing.
methodology_description: The authors propose and evaluate a Matrix Product State (MPS) based generative model to learn and reproduce time-series (price-path) distributions from a stochastic volatility model (Heston). They first generate training data by simulating the Heston SDEs with an Euler–Maruyama discretization (with reflection to avoid negative variance). Continuous asset prices are linearly quantized to m-bit integers (physical dimension 2^m). An MPS (a chain of rank-3 tensors) is used to represent the joint amplitude over the discretized time-series; probabilities are given by normalized squared amplitudes. Training minimizes the KL divergence (implemented as negative log-likelihood) using a sweeping (DMRG-like) algorithm: adjacent tensor pairs are merged, gradients of the loss to the merged tensor are computed, updated by gradient descent, then SVD is performed and singular values are truncated (with an upper bound D_max) to update/tune bond dimensions. After training, the model draws full-path samples by sequentially computing marginals and conditional probabilities (exact contraction of MPS legs) and sampling each time-step integer, then mapping integers back to real prices. The sampled paths are used in classical Monte Carlo to estimate option prices (European, Asian, lookback, up-and-out barrier); European prices are inverted to Black–Scholes implied volatility for comparison. Experiments vary quantization bits m and maximum bond dimension D_max and compare generated distributions and option prices (with standard errors) against the baseline Heston-simulated paths.
algorithms_used: Sweeping / DMRG-like training (merge adjacent tensors, update, SVD truncation)
Gradient descent optimization on negative log-likelihood (KL divergence)
Sequential marginal / conditional sampling from MPS
dataset_used: Synthetic price-path data generated from the Heston stochastic volatility model via Euler–Maruyama discretization. N=10,000 simulated sample paths, each with M=5 time points (daily step Δt = 1/250). Heston parameters: κ=1.0, θ=0.04, ξ=2, ρ=-0.7, S0=100, v0=0.04. Prices were linearly rescaled and quantized to m-bit integers (m varied).

experiment_input.preprocessing: Linear min-max scaling of each path value to integer grid {0,...,2^m-1} with m in {4,5,6}; reflection applied to enforce nonnegative variance during Euler–Maruyama; Smin/Smax taken from training samples for scaling.

steps: Simulate N=10000 paths of the Heston model using Euler–Maruyama with reflection for negative variances.
Rescale and quantize each continuous price St to m-bit integer ¯St in {0,...,2^m-1} via linear mapping using training-set min/max.
Construct an MPS representing the amplitude Ψ(¯x1,...,¯xM) with physical dimension 2^m and trainable bond dimensions (bounded by D_max).

Train by minimizing negative log-likelihood (equivalent to KL divergence): perform sweeping updates—merge adjacent tensors A(j) and A(j+1), compute gradient of loss w.r.t. merged tensor, update by gradient descent, apply SVD to merged tensor and truncate singular values up to D_max, and redistribute factors to form updated rank-3 tensors. Repeat sweeps (epochs) until convergence.

After training, generate samples by sequential sampling: compute marginal P(¯x1) via contraction, sample ¯x1; compute P(¯x2|¯x1), sample ¯x2, etc., to obtain full discretized path; convert integers back to real-valued prices.
Price options (European, Asian, Lookback, Up-and-out barrier with K=100, B=105 for barrier) using classical Monte Carlo on the generated paths (N=10000).
For European option, invert Black–Scholes formula to obtain implied volatility for comparison versus baseline.
experiment_process.notes: Learning rate η and number of training epochs / convergence criteria are not specified in the manuscript.

experiment_output.format: Empirical probability distributions (histograms / KDE) of asset price at selected time points; option price estimates (Monte Carlo averages) with standard errors computed over 10 independent runs; European implied volatility values derived from option prices.
experiment_output.baselines: Direct Monte Carlo simulation of the Heston model (same discretization) used as ground-truth baseline for distributions and option prices.

experiment_parameters.optimization_method: Gradient descent with sweeping (DMRG-like updates); SVD truncation

key_findings: [supported] A Matrix Product State (MPS) generative model can be trained to reproduce joint distributions of short asset-price time series generated by the Heston stochastic volatility model and can be used to draw synthetic paths.

[supported] Increasing the MPS physical dimension (m) and the maximum bond dimension (Dmax) improves the agreement between distributions and option prices produced from MPS-generated paths and those produced from the original Heston model.

[supported] For the experiments performed (M = 5 time steps, N = 10,000 training paths, Euler–Maruyama discretization with Δt = 1/250), the MPS model with m = 6 and Dmax = 150 produced European, Asian and Lookback option prices close to those obtained from the Heston model, while the up-and-out barrier option showed larger discrepancies.

[supported] The authors trained the MPS using a negative log-likelihood objective (KL divergence) and a DMRG-like sweeping algorithm with SVD-based bond-dimension truncation; this training procedure adapted bond dimensions and produced usable models.
[supported] Exact sample generation from the trained MPS is computationally tractable classically via sequential marginal/conditional probability evaluation (no MCMC required).

[supported] Numerical experiment details and quantitative outputs are provided (e.g., European call price and implied volatility comparisons between Heston and MPS models for various m and Dmax settings).

[speculative] The MPS representation learned classically can be compiled into an efficient quantum circuit to prepare a quantum state encoding the joint path distribution, potentially reducing the state-preparation cost required by Quantum Monte Carlo / Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QMCI/QAE) workflows for option pricing.
[speculative] The MPS-based generative approach could be extended to other stochastic asset models (e.g., CEV, SABR) and used in end-to-end quantum implementations for path-dependent option pricing.

[speculative] Further improvements (larger m, larger/other tensor-network architectures, regularization) may reduce observed discrepancies for path-dependent payoffs that are sensitive to rare events (e.g., barrier options).
results_summary: The paper proposes using Matrix Product States (MPS) as a generative model for discretized asset-price time series and demonstrates, via classical numerical experiments on the Heston stochastic-volatility model, that MPS can learn and sample joint distributions for short paths (M=5) from N=10,000 training trajectories. Quantitatively, increasing the MPS physical dimension and bond dimension improves fit: with m=6 (64-level discretization) and Dmax=150, MPS-generated paths yield European, Asian and Lookback option prices close to those obtained from the Heston model, though barrier option prices remain less accurate. The authors argue (speculatively) that such classically-trained MPS representations can be efficiently compiled into quantum circuits to address the costly state-preparation step in QMCI-based quantum option pricing, but do not implement or benchmark the quantum circuit nor demonstrate a runtime or gate-count advantage.
performance_claims: Training and evaluation used N = 10,000 Heston sample paths, M = 5 time steps, Euler–Maruyama with Δt = 1/250.
Heston benchmark European call price: 1.1098 (standard error 0.0052); implied volatility (IV): 0.1967 (0.0009).
Heston benchmark Asian option price: 0.6195 (0.0035); corresponding MPS (m=6,Dmax=150): 0.6107 (0.0026).
Heston benchmark Lookback option price: 1.4778 (0.0056); corresponding MPS (m=6,Dmax=150): 1.4612 (0.0049).
Heston benchmark Barrier (up-and-out) option price: 0.9894 (0.0049); corresponding MPS (m=6,Dmax=150): 0.9160 (0.0030), showing a larger discrepancy.
Increasing Dmax from 64 to 150 (with m=6) moved MPS European call prices from 0.9767 (Dmax=64) to 1.0321 (Dmax=100) to 1.0805 (Dmax=150), approaching the Heston benchmark.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not demonstrate a quantum runtime or gate-count advantage experimentally. It motivates the approach by citing the theoretical quadratic speedup of Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QMCI/QAE) for Monte Carlo integration and proposes, speculatively, that classically-trained MPS models can be compiled into efficient quantum circuits to reduce state-preparation costs. The potential for quantum advantage is argued conceptually but not empirically validated or benchmarked in the work.
limitations: State-preparation (oracle P) on quantum devices may be computationally demanding and the paper does not provide an implemented quantum end-to-end pipeline.
Experiments are limited to a single stochastic model (Heston); generality to other models is not demonstrated.
MPS models were trained and validated classically; no implementation or resource analysis of the corresponding quantum circuit was provided.
Time series length is small (M = 5); scalability to longer time horizons / more time steps was not studied.
Discretization of continuous prices into m-bit integers introduces approximation error; small m yields poor fidelity to target distribution (coarse grids).
Model capacity controlled by bond-dimension (Dmax) limits expressive power; some option prices (notably barrier option) remain poorly matched even with increased Dmax.
MPS had difficulty accurately pricing barrier options (sensitivity to tail events and path-dependent conditions), indicating potential weakness in modeling rare/outlier events.
No rigorous error bounds or theoretical guarantees relating MPS approximation quality to option pricing error were provided.

Training uses ad-hoc choices (Euler–Maruyama discretization, reflection rule for negative variance) which may introduce biases; effects of numerical discretization schemes were not explored. [inferred]

Only a limited set of option types were evaluated; applicability to a wider array of path-dependent or multi-asset derivatives was not tested. [inferred]
Generalization behavior (overfitting/underfitting) of trained MPS to out-of-sample market regimes or different parameter settings was not assessed. [inferred]

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Matrix Product State (MPS) generative models can learn joint path distributions for short asset time series and be used to produce synthetic paths for pricing path-dependent derivatives, positioning MPS as a candidate for efficient quantum state preparation for quantum Monte Carlo option pricing.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The workflow is hybrid: classical simulation (Heston) generates training data, a classically-trained MPS represents the joint distribution (quantum-inspired model / state), and classical Monte Carlo prices options on the generated paths; authors argue this MPS representation could enable downstream quantum Monte Carlo.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Experiments use small time-series (M=5) and modest quantization (m≤6) yielding an implicitly small qubit footprint (m*M up to ~30), suggesting potential near-term applicability for short-path problems or as a proof-of-concept for state preparation techniques.

#limitation:data-encoding — Continuous prices are linearly quantized to m-bit integers using min/max from training data; this discretization and reliance on dataset min/max for scaling are identified as important factors affecting fidelity and generalization.

#limitation:qubit-count — Experiments are restricted to short sequences (M=5) and small m; scaling to longer maturities or finer price resolution would increase physical dimension and required bond dimension, posing scalability challenges.

#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments and training are classical (MPS contractions and sampling performed classically); no experiments were performed on quantum hardware to validate the claimed quantum state-preparation benefits.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Higher physical dimension (m) and larger bond-dimension (D_max) improve distributional and pricing agreement with baseline Heston Monte Carlo, indicating controllable trade-offs between model size and fidelity.
